sentences.text: For five episodes, one phrase has followed every number: rough estimates.
The step is 2.02. Alder sits 0.87 above Cedar. Rough, we said, and moved on.
Today we pay that debt.
The dial reads 2.02, which multiplies the odds by seven and a half. Would you stake much on seven and a half? On somewhere between five and ten?
Hold your guess. The answer is in the shape of the hill.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: how sure are we?
Here is the hill from Episode 6: the height for each position of the dial.
Its top is at 2.02. The question is how far from the top the truth could be.
That depends on how sharply the top is curved. A sharp peak pins the dial. A flat one lets it wander.
And we already have the curvature. It is the folded number from last time: 2.93.
One over its square root gives the standard error: 0.58.
Go about two of those either side of the top, and you have a 95% interval: from 0.87 to 3.16.
As a multiplier on the odds, that is anywhere from 2.4 to 23.6.
So the data are clear that higher risk raises the odds. They cannot say whether by a factor of two or of twenty.
Could the true step be zero? The hill answers in three ways.
Across: zero lies about three and a half standard errors from the top.
Down: the hill at zero stands 7.3 below the top.
And by the slope: at zero, the ground is still climbing steeply.
Three different measurements, one verdict. A step this large would turn up by chance less than once in a thousand.
Now the clinics. Each one has a little hill of its own, and its curvature is that clinic's wobble.
Alder's is 6.38, so on its own its standard error is 0.40. Dune's is 2.31: 0.66.
Notice what earns precision. Not the number of patients, but what each patient adds: most near 50%, almost nothing near zero or a hundred.
Elm has 11 patients and a wobble of 0.02. A hundred patients at 2% would carry less than Dune's twelve.
But a clinic's gamma is not read on its own. It is read where the risk factor is zero, and getting there leans on the dial.
Birch's patients are mostly higher-risk, so its gamma at zero borrows heavily: 0.65, against 0.39 on its own. Alder barely borrows: 0.41 against 0.40.
And here zero bites again. Record the risk factor three units higher, and Alder's standard error swells to 1.9, though no gap between clinics has changed.
So read each clinic where the patients actually are: at the average case mix.
There the standard errors are 0.43, 0.47, 0.52 and 0.66, however the risk factor is recorded. These are the ones a fair comparison needs.
Put it in one picture. Each clinic's gamma, with its 95% interval.
Every interval overlaps every other.
With 103 patients, the model has an opinion about the order of these clinics, and very little confidence in it.
And Elm. Its printed interval runs from minus 19.7 to plus 7.2. That is not an estimate. It is a warning sign.
One caution about the picture. Each interval is about one clinic. Whether two clinics differ is a separate calculation, and it comes later.
So what would it take to be sure? Ask the crowd.
Among its 200 providers, those with 20 to 30 patients have a standard error near 0.55. Near 100 patients: 0.26. Above 400: 0.12.
Four times the patients, half the error.
For a standard error of 0.1 at a 20% readmission rate, a provider needs about 625 patients.
Let's gather it up.
A sharp peak means a small standard error: one over the square root of the curvature.
A clinic's uncertainty is its own, plus a share of the dial's.
And for a fair comparison, read every clinic at the average case mix.
All of it assumes patients are independent of one another. Count the same patient twice, and these intervals are too narrow.
We have left one clinic waiting since Episode 4. Next time: Elm.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
